entities.name: Leonhard von Keutschach
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Leonhard von Keutschach, who governed as Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg from 1495 until his death on June 18, 1519, stands as a pivotal figure in the late medieval Holy Roman Empire, embodying the twilight of feudal ecclesiastical rule. His episcopacy marked the apex of Salzburg's territorial sovereignty, transforming the archdiocese into a formidable political and economic power, largely independent from both Bavarian and Habsburg influence. Keutschach was a shrewd politician and administrator, consolidating princely power and leaving an indelible mark on the region's governance and infrastructure, even as the broader European landscape shifted towards early modern statecraft and the Reformation loomed.

During his 24-year reign, Keutschach effectively suppressed a series of peasant uprisings, notably the "Käse-Rebellion" of 1497 and the larger "Pongau Rebellion" of 1511-1513, through a combination of military force and strategic negotiation, thereby securing the stability of his domain. He meticulously reformed the archiepiscopal finances, acquiring vital salt mines in Hallein and initiating a significant coinage reform that enriched the treasury. His architectural patronage included the extensive rebuilding of Hohensalzburg Fortress, transforming it into one of Europe's most imposing strongholds, and the construction of new administrative buildings, symbolizing his temporal authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Leonhard von Keutschach significantly shaped the regional history of Salzburg, transforming it into a powerful and autonomous principality through shrewd administration and military strength, influencing its economic and political trajectory for centuries. His actions also contributed to the social tensions that led to the wider German Peasants' War.
